nodes.name: Partition regularity
nodes.statement: Let F be a number field, or a subset of some number field. An equation p(x,y,n)colon F^3rightarrowC is partition regular in F if for any partition of F into finitely many disjoint sets, for some nin F, one of the cells contains distinct x and y that satisfy p(x,y,n)=0.
nodes.raw_latex:
Let $\mathbb{F}$ be a number field, or a subset of some number field. An equation $p(x,y,n)\colon \mathbb{F}^{3}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is \emph{partition regular} in $\mathbb{F}$ if
  for any partition of $\mathbb{F}$ into finitely many disjoint sets, for some $n\in \mathbb{F}$, one of the cells contains distinct $x$ and $y$ that satisfy $p(x,y,n)=0$.

nodes.name: Smooth sequences
nodes.statement: Given a nilmanifold G/Gamma, MinN, and vecN=(N_1,dots,N_t)inN^t, we say that the sequence epsiloncolon[vecN]rightarrow G is (M,vecN)-smooth if for every vecnin[vecN], we have d_G(epsilon(vecn),bold1_G)leq M and d_G(epsilon(vecn),epsilon(vecn-vece_i))leq M/N_i for all 1leq ileq t, where the i-th coordinate of vece_i is 1 and all other coordinates are 0.

Let the integers $M_{1}, M$ and the nilmanifold $X'=G'/\Gamma'\in\mathcal{F}
(M)$ be given by Theorem \ref{mFo}. Note that the sequence
$(g(m,n))_{(m,n)\in[\tilde{N}]\times[\tilde{N}]}$ is a degree 2 polynomial sequence in $G$
with respect to the filtration $G_{\bullet}$. Let
$(g'(m,n))_{(m,n)\in[\tilde{N}]\times[\tilde{N}]}$ be the sequence given by the decomposition
of Theorem \ref{mFo}. By Lemma \ref{2p}, we can write
\begin{equation}\nonumber
  \begin{split}
  g'(m,n)=g_{0}g_{1,1}^{m}g_{1,2}^{n}g_{2,1}^{\binom{m}{2}}g_{2,2}^{mn}g_{2,3}^{\binom{n}{2}}
  \end{split}
\end{equation}
for some $g_{0}, g_{1,1}, g_{1,2}\in G, g_{2,1},g_{2,2},g_{2,3}\in G_{2}$.
It remains to show that
$g_{0}, g_{1,1}, g_{1,2}\in G'$, $g_{2,1},g_{2,2},g_{2,3}\in G'_{2}$
for case (ii).

Since $g_{0}=g(0,0)$, we have $g_{0}\in G'$. So the sequence
$g''(m,n)=g_{0}^{-1}g'(m,n)$ also takes values in $G'$.
Denote
$$\partial_{(x,y)}g(m,n)=g(m+x,n+y)g(m,n)^{-1}.$$ Since $G$ is of order 2,
$G_{2}$ is included in the center of $G$. Therefore, we obtain
\begin{equation}\nonumber
  \begin{split}
  \partial_{(1,0)}g''(m,0)=g_{1,1}g_{2,1}^{m} \text{ and }
  \partial_{(1,0)}^{2}g''(m,0)=g_{2,1}.
  \end{split}
\end{equation}
It follows that $g_{1,1},g_{2,1}\in G'$. Similarly,
$g_{1,2},g_{2,3}\in G'$. Thus the sequence
$g'''(m,n)=g_{2,2}^{m,n}$ also takes values in $G'$, which implies
$g_{2,2}\in G'$.

If we are in case (i), then $G'$ is abelian and we are done. If
$G'$ is not abelian, then $G'_{2}$ is a non-trivial subgroup of $G_{2}$.
Moreover, $G'_{2}$ is closed and connected, and by hypothesis $G_{2}$
is isomorphic to the torus $\mathbb{T}$. It follows that $G'_{2}=G_{2}$.
Hence $g_{2,1},g_{2,2},g_{2,3}\in G'_{2}$. This finishes the proof.

nodes.statement: An element boldk=(k_1,dots,k_2s+2)inZ^2s+2 is said to be a vector of type 1 if k_2s+1=k_2s+2=0 and of type 2 if k_2s+2=0. Every boldkinZ^2s+2 is said to be a vector of type 3. For any subgroup H of H_0, boldkinZ^2s+2 is said to be of the same type as H if both boldk and H are of type j for some j=1,2,3.
nodes.raw_latex:
An element $\bold{k}=(k_{1},\dots,k_{2s+2})\in\mathbb{Z}^{2s+2}$ is said to be a vector of \emph{type 1} if $k_{2s+1}=k_{2s+2}=0$ and of \emph{type 2} if $k_{2s+2}=0$. Every
$\bold{k}\in\mathbb{Z}^{2s+2}$ is said to be a vector of \emph{type 3}. For any subgroup $H$ of $H_{0}$, $\bold{k}\in\mathbb{Z}^{2s+2}$ is said to be \emph{of the same type as} $H$
if both $\bold{k}$ and $H$ are of type $j$ for some $j=1,2,3$.

For any subgroup H of H_0, boldkinZ^2s+2 is said to be of the same type as H if both boldk and H are of type j for some j=1,2,3.

\label{appro2}(Approximation property).
Let $\bold{\lambda}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, \bold{\lambda}\neq(0,0)$. Set $\tilde{\alpha}=\theta^{-1}_{\bold{\lambda}}\alpha$.
Let $H$ be a subgroup of $H_{0}$. For every $C,D,\kappa>0, d\in\mathbb{N}$, there exist $C'=C'(X,C,\kappa,d), \kappa'=\kappa'(X,C,\kappa,d), D'=D'(X,C,D,\kappa,d)>0, N_{0}=N_{0}(X,C,\kappa,d)\in\mathbb{N}$ with the following property: Let $N\geq N_{0}$. Suppose that $g_{1}(n)=\prod_{i=0}^{d}\alpha_{i}^{\binom{n}{i}}, \alpha_{0},\dots,\alpha_{d-1}\in H, \alpha_{d}\in H_{2}$ is a $d$-polynomial which is not $S$-totally $\kappa$-equidistributed on $H$. Suppose also that
  $\bold{k}=p\underline{\bold{k}}\in\mathbb{Z}^{2s+2}$ is a vector of the same type as $H$ such that
   $H$ and $H^{\underline{\bold{k}}}$ are $\bold{\lambda}$-shaped,
   and that
   $0<\Vert\bold{k}\Vert\leq C, \Vert\bold{k}\cdot\tilde{\alpha_{i}}\Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}\leq\frac{C}{N^{i}}$ for all $1\leq i\leq d-1$.

  Suppose that both $H$ and $H^{\underline{\bold{k}}}$ are $\bold{\lambda}$-shaped.
  Then there exists a polynomial sequence of the form $g_{2}(n)=\prod_{i=0}^{d}\beta_{i}^{\binom{n}{i}}$, $\beta_{0},\dots,\beta_{d}\in H^{\underline{\bold{k}}}$ such that

  1) If the pair $(H,H^{\underline{\bold{k}}})$ is good, then $g_{2}$ is not $S$-totally $\kappa'$-equidistributed on $H^{\underline{\bold{k}}}$;

2) If there exists $\bold{p}\in\mathbb{Z}^{2s+2}$ of the same type as $H$ (and thus of $H^{\underline{\bold{k}}}$) such that $0<\Vert\bold{p}\Vert\leq D$ and $\Vert\bold{p}\cdot\tilde{\beta_{1}}\Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}\leq\frac{D}{N}$,
then there exists some $w\in\mathbb{Z}, 0<w\leq C^{2}$ such that $\Vert w\bold{p}\cdot\tilde{\alpha_{1}}\Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}\leq\frac{D'}{N}$.

3) If $H_{2}=H_{2}^{\underline{\bold{k}}}$, then $\beta_{d}\in H_{2}^{\underline{\bold{k}}}$.

nodes.name: Height
nodes.statement: The height of a rational number fracpq (p,qinZ,(p,q)=1) is max\vert pvert,vert qvert\. We denote the height of an irrational number to be infty. The height of a matrix is the maximum of the heights of entries of M. If A is a subspace of R^n with dimension r, let C(A) denote the collection of all ntimes r matrices B such that A can be written as A=\BvectinR^ncolonvectinR^r\. The height of A is the minimum of the heights of BinC(A). Since the integers are discrete, the height of A is always well-defined.

The \emph{height} of a rational number $\frac{p}{q} (p,q\in\mathbb{Z},(p,q)=1)$ is $\max\{\vert p\vert,\vert q\vert\}$. We denote the height of an irrational number to be $\infty$.

  The \emph{height} of a matrix is the maximum of the heights of entries of $M$.

  If $A$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ with dimension $r$, let $\mathcal{C}(A)$ denote the collection of all $n\times r$ matrices $B$ such that $A$ can
  be written as $A=\{B\vec{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\colon\vec{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{r}\}$. The \emph{height} of $A$ is the minimum of the heights of $B\in\mathcal{C}(A)$. Since the integers are discrete, the height of $A$ is always well-defined.

nodes.name: Non-trivial vector
nodes.statement: Let A be a subspace and boldv be a vector of R^n. We say that boldv is non-trivial with respect to A if A is not contained in the orthogonal complement of boldv. In particular, boldv is non-trivial with respect to R^n if and only if boldvneq bold0.

where $F_{4}=D'_{1}(F_{1}\cdot D'_{2}(\dots F_{1}\cdot D'_{i}(0)\dots))$. So the existence of $\eta_{1}$ in (i) is proved.
The existence of $\eta_{2}$ in (i) holds similarly and therefore conclusion (i) holds.

If $rank(A)= s$, by a simple computation using linear algebra, (\ref{ABA2}) implies that $B^{G}=0$. So $G$ is abelian, a contradiction.

\

If the pair $(H_{i},H_{i+1})$ is not good, by Lemma \ref{good}, we must have that $H_{i}$ is of type 1 and $H_{i+1}$ is of type 2,
and $H_{i+1}$ must be $(1,1)$-shaped. By a similar discussion,
we can still construct the system $Y_{i+1}$ and the sequence $h_{i+1}$ such that $(II),(III)$ and $(IV)$ hold (but $(I)$ may not hold).
Set $r=2s-i+1$. Since in this case $\bold{v}_{j}$ is of type 1 for all $0\leq j\leq i$, $H_{i+1}$ can be written as
\begin{equation}\nonumber
 \begin{split}
  H_{i+1}=\Bigl\{ (\bold{t}A,w;\bold{t}A',w')\colon\bold{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{r}, w,w'\in\mathbb{R}\Bigr\},
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
where $A$ and $A'$ are some full rank $r\times s$ matrices with height at most $F_{1}$. By Lemma \ref{dege}, we have that
\begin{equation}\nonumber
 \begin{split}
  [H_{i+1},H_{i+1}]=\Bigl\{ (\bold{0},\bold{s}AB^{G}A^{T}\bold{t}^{T};\bold{0},\bold{s}A'B^{G}A'^{T}\bold{t}^{T})\colon\bold{s},\bold{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{r}\Bigr\}.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
So we deduce that
\begin{equation}\label{ABA}
 \begin{split}
  AB^{G}A^{T}=A'B^{G}A'^{T}.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}

If $rank(A)<s$, similar to the previous case, there exist $F_{3}>0$ and $\bold{p}=(\bold{p}_{0},\bold{0})\in\mathbb{Z}^{s}\times\{0\}^{s+2}$ with $0<\Vert\bold{p}\Vert\leq F_{3}$ such that
$\Vert\bold{p}\cdot\tilde{\bold{c}_{i+1}}\Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}=\Vert\bold{p}_{0}\cdot\widehat{\bold{a}_{i+1}}\Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}\leq\frac{F_{3}}{N}$.
Since the coefficients of each pair $(h_{j},h_{j+1}) (0\leq j\leq i)$ satisfy Property 2) of Lemma \ref{appro2} and $\bold{p}$ is of type 1 (and thus is of the same type
as all subgroups of $H_{0}$), there exists
$w\in\mathbb{Z}$ with $0<\vert w\vert\leq F_{4}$ such that
$\Vert w\bold{p}\cdot\tilde{\bold{c}_{0}}\Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}=\Vert w\bold{p}_{0}\cdot\widehat{\bold{a}_{0}}\Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}\leq\frac{F_{4}}{N}$,
where $F_{4}=D'_{1}(F_{1}\cdot D'_{2}(\dots F_{1}\cdot D'_{i}(0)\dots))$. So the existence of $\eta_{1}$ in (i) is proved.
The existence of $\eta_{2}$ in (i) holds similarly and therefore conclustion (i) holds.

Now we assume that $rank(A)=s$. In this case $r\geq s$. Suppose that $A'=Y\binom{I_{s\times s}}{0_{(r-s)\times s}}$ for some
invertible $r\times r$ matrix $Y$. Denote $A=Y\binom{A_{1}}{A_{2}}$, where $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$ are respectively $s\times s$ and $(r-s)\times s$ matrices.
Then (\ref{ABA}) implies that
\begin{equation}\nonumber
 \begin{split}
  & A_{1}B^{G}A_{1}^{T}=B^{G};
  \\& A_{2}B^{G}(A_{1}^{T},A_{2}^{T})=0.
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Note that $A_{1}B^{G}A_{1}^{T}=B^{G}$ implies that $A_{1}^{T}\in\Lambda(B^{G})$. Since $rank(A)=s$, $A_{2}B^{G}(A_{1}^{T},A_{2}^{T})=0$ implies that $A_{2}B^{G}=0$. Let $A''$ be the upper left $s'\times s'$ block of the matrix $A_{1}^{T}$. Since $A_{1}^{T}\in\Lambda(B^{G})$, we deduce that $A''\in\Lambda(B_{0}^{G})$.

Suppose that $\widehat{\bold{a}_{i+1}}=\bold{t}A, \widehat{\bold{b}_{i+1}}=\bold{t}A'$ for some $\bold{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{r}$. Then
$\widehat{\bold{a}_{i+1}}=\bold{s}\binom{A_{1}}{A_{2}}, \widehat{\bold{b}_{i+1}}=\bold{s}\binom{I_{s\times s}}{0_{s\times (r-s)}}$, where $\bold{s}=\bold{t}Y$. Denote $\bold{s}=(\bold{s}_{1},\bold{s}_{2}), \bold{s}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{s}, \bold{s}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{r-s}$.
Then $\widehat{\bold{b}_{i+1}}=\bold{s}_{1}, \widehat{\bold{a}_{i+1}}=\bold{s}_{1}A_{1}+\bold{s}_{2}A_{2}=\widehat{\bold{b}_{i+1}}A_{1}+\bold{s}_{2}A_{2}$. So $\widehat{\bold{a}_{i+1}}B^{G}=\widehat{\bold{b}_{i+1}}A_{1}B^{G}$.
Thus
$\widehat{\bold{a}_{i+1}}B^{G}A_{1}^{T}=\widehat{\bold{b}_{i+1}}A_{1}B^{G}A_{1}^{T}= \widehat{\bold{b}_{i+1}}B^{G}$.
Suppose that $\bold{s}_{3}\in\mathbb{R}^{s'}$ is the vector consisting of the first $s'$ entries of $\bold{s}_{1}$. Then
considering the first $s'$ entries of $\widehat{\bold{a}_{i+1}}B^{G}A_{1}^{T}$ and $\widehat{\bold{b}_{i+1}}B^{G}$, we get that
$\bold{a}_{i+1}^{\bullet}B_{0}^{G}A''=\bold{b}_{i+1}^{\bullet}B_{0}^{G}$.
Since the coefficients of each pair $(h_{j},h_{j+1}) (0\leq j\leq i)$ satisfy Property 2) of Lemma \ref{appro2}, we
deduce that $\bold{a}^{\bullet}B_{0}^{G}A''$ is at most $\frac{F_{5}}{N}$-away from $\bold{b}^{\bullet}B_{0}^{G}$ for some $F_{3}>0$ depending only on $X$ and $\kappa$, and $A''\in\Lambda(B_{0}^{G})$ is of height at most $F_{5}$. Therefore, conclusion
(ii) holds.
